hook.text: 99% uptime sounds great until you realize that's 3.65 days of downtime per year. Five nines means 5 minutes.

buildup.text: Availability is measured in nines: 99% (two nines), 99.9% (three nines), 99.99% (four nines), 99.999% (five nines).

discovery.text: Each additional nine is 10x harder to achieve. Going from 99.9% to 99.99% requires fundamentally different architecture.

twist.text: Not everything needs five nines. An internal admin panel at 99% is fine. A payment system at 99% would be a disaster.

climax.text: Availability targets should match business impact. Over-engineering wastes money; under-engineering loses customers.

punchline.text: Each additional nine is 10x harder and 10x more expensive.

quiz.question: How much downtime does 99.9% availability allow per year?

hook.text: Your cloud provider promises 99.99% uptime. What happens if they miss it? That's what an SLA defines.

buildup.text: SLI is the measured metric (actual uptime). SLO is the target (99.9%). SLA is the contract with consequences if missed.

discovery.text: SLOs should be stricter than SLAs. If your SLA promises 99.9%, set your SLO at 99.95% to have a safety margin.

twist.text: SLAs often promise credits, not refunds. If AWS is down for a day, you get 10% off next month — not lost revenue back.

climax.text: SLIs measure reality, SLOs set internal goals, SLAs set external promises. All three must align.

punchline.text: SLI measures it, SLO targets it, SLA promises it.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between SLO and SLA?
options: SLO is the internal target, SLA is the external contractual promise

hook.text: Your SLO is 99.9% uptime. That means you're allowed 43 minutes of downtime per month. That's your error budget.

buildup.text: An error budget is the acceptable amount of unreliability. It's calculated as 100% minus the SLO target.

discovery.text: When the error budget is full, ship features fast. When it's depleted, freeze features and focus on reliability.

twist.text: Error budgets align incentives: product teams want speed, reliability teams want stability. The budget is shared.

climax.text: Error budgets turn reliability from an abstract goal into a concrete, measurable resource that teams can spend.

punchline.text: Reliability is a budget — spend it wisely on velocity.

quiz.question: What happens when the error budget is depleted?
options: Feature releases freeze and the team focuses on reliability

hook.text: Your system fails every 30 days but recovers in 5 minutes. Better than failing every 90 days with a 4-hour recovery?

buildup.text: MTTF measures how long until something breaks. MTTR measures how fast you recover. Together they define availability.

discovery.text: Low MTTR is often more valuable than high MTTF. You can't prevent all failures, but you can recover fast.

twist.text: MTTR includes detection time. If nobody notices for 2 hours, your MTTR is already 2 hours before you start fixing.

climax.text: Investing in detection and recovery (lower MTTR) often gives better availability than preventing failures (higher MTTF).

punchline.text: Recover fast beats fail rarely — invest in MTTR.

quiz.question: Why is MTTR often more important than MTTF?
options: You can't prevent all failures, but you can recover from them quickly

hook.text: Your average response time is 100ms. But 1% of users wait 5 seconds. The average hides the worst experiences.

buildup.text: P50 is the median: half of requests are faster, half are slower. P99 is the latency that 99% of requests beat.

discovery.text: Amazon found that every 100ms of latency costs 1% of sales. P99 matters because your worst experience defines trust.

twist.text: P99.9 can be 100x worse than P50. A GC pause, a cold cache, or a retry storm hits only a few users — hard.

climax.text: Measure P50 for typical experience and P99 for worst-case. Optimizing averages ignores the users who suffer most.

punchline.text: Averages lie — measure P99 to see the worst experience.

quiz.question: Why is P99 latency more important than average latency?
options: It reveals the worst experience that 1% of users suffer

hook.text: Hardware dies, software crashes, networks partition, and humans err. Failure isn't a bug — it's a feature of reality.

buildup.text: Hardware failures: disk dies, server loses power. Software failures: memory leak, infinite loop, null pointer.

discovery.text: Network: packets lost, connections timeout, DNS dies. Human error: wrong config pushed, wrong database deleted.

twist.text: The most common failure type is human error — misconfigured deployments cause more outages than hardware combined.

climax.text: Reliable systems assume failure is normal and design to survive it, not prevent it.

punchline.text: Everything fails — design to survive, not to prevent.

quiz.question: What is the most common cause of system outages?

hook.text: One database, one DNS server, one load balancer. If any single one dies, everything goes down.

buildup.text: A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose failure brings down the entire system.

discovery.text: Eliminate SPOFs by adding redundancy: multiple database replicas, multiple DNS providers, multiple load balancers.

twist.text: Redundancy introduces complexity. Two databases must stay in sync. Failover logic must work correctly — and be tested.

climax.text: Map every component in your architecture. If any single one failing causes total outage, that's your SPOF to fix.

punchline.text: If one component dying takes everything down, it's a SPOF.

quiz.question: How do you eliminate a single point of failure?
options: Add redundancy so no single component's failure causes total outage

hook.text: One server slows down. Traffic shifts to the rest. They overload and slow down too. Everything crashes.

buildup.text: A cascading failure starts small and spreads as failing components put more load on healthy ones, which then also fail.

discovery.text: The 2003 Northeast blackout was a cascade: one power line failed, shifting load until the entire grid collapsed.

twist.text: Retries accelerate cascades. A slow service gets retry storms — 3x the load from retries — making it even slower.

climax.text: Preventing cascades requires circuit breakers, load shedding, and retry budgets to stop failures from spreading.

punchline.text: One failure overloads the rest — cascading failures take down everything.

quiz.question: What accelerates cascading failures?
options: Retry storms that add more load to already failing services

hook.text: The server is running. Health checks pass. But 10% of requests fail silently. It's not up or down — it's gray.

buildup.text: Gray failures are partial: the system works for most requests but fails for some. Health checks don't catch them.

discovery.text: A disk with increasing read errors, a network dropping 5% of packets, or a process leaking memory — all gray failures.

twist.text: Gray failures are harder to detect than total ones. The system looks healthy by most metrics but users suffer.

climax.text: Detecting gray failures requires deep health checks: test real user paths, not just that the process is running.

punchline.text: Not fully down, not fully up — gray failures hide in plain sight.

quiz.question: Why are gray failures hard to detect?
options: The system appears healthy by basic metrics but fails partially for some users

hook.text: A bad deploy reaches all servers in 60 seconds. Every user is affected instantly. The blast radius is 100%.

buildup.text: Blast radius is the scope of impact when something goes wrong. Smaller blast radius means fewer affected users.

discovery.text: Canary deployments limit blast radius: deploy to 1% of servers first. If it fails, only 1% of users are affected.

twist.text: Cell-based architecture isolates users into independent cells. A failure in one cell doesn't affect other cells.

climax.text: Minimizing blast radius is the most effective way to limit the damage of inevitable failures.

punchline.text: Contain the explosion — limit how many users a failure affects.

quiz.question: How do canary deployments reduce blast radius?
options: By deploying to a small percentage of servers first before rolling out fully
By testing in a staging environment

hook.text: A downstream service is down. Your service keeps calling it, waiting for timeouts. Every request takes 30s and fails.

buildup.text: A circuit breaker monitors failures. After a threshold of consecutive failures, it opens — blocking all calls instantly.

discovery.text: When open, calls fail instantly without waiting. After a cooldown, one test request checks if the service recovered.

twist.text: Without circuit breakers, a slow dependency slows your service too. With them, you fail fast and gracefully degrade.

climax.text: Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures by isolating unhealthy dependencies and failing fast instead of waiting.

punchline.text: Fail fast when a dependency is down — don't wait and suffer.

quiz.question: What does an open circuit breaker do?
options: Blocks all calls to the failing service and returns errors immediately
Routes traffic to a different service

hook.text: Your request fails. You retry immediately. It fails again. You retry again. You're now hammering a struggling service.

buildup.text: Exponential backoff adds increasing delays between retries: 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s. Each retry waits longer.

discovery.text: Adding jitter randomizes the delay so thousands of clients don't all retry at the same millisecond.

twist.text: Retries without backoff create retry storms that worsen outages. The retries become the attack on the struggling server.

climax.text: Exponential backoff with jitter is the standard retry strategy for every network call in distributed systems.

punchline.text: Wait longer between retries, add randomness — don't pile on.

quiz.question: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
options: To prevent thousands of clients from retrying at the exact same moment
To reduce the number of retries

hook.text: A ship has bulkheads: sealed compartments. If one floods, the others stay dry. The ship survives.

buildup.text: In software, bulkheads isolate components. If the image service fails, it shouldn't take down the checkout flow.

discovery.text: Separate thread pools per dependency. If one pool is exhausted waiting on a slow service, others keep working.

twist.text: Without bulkheads, one slow API consumes all available threads. Every other API endpoint becomes unresponsive too.

climax.text: Bulkheads contain failures to their compartment, preventing one bad component from sinking the entire system.

punchline.text: Isolate components — one failure shouldn't sink the whole ship.

quiz.question: What is a bulkhead pattern in software?
options: Isolating components so one failure doesn't affect the rest of the system

hook.text: The recommendation engine is down. Do you show an error page? Or show the page without recommendations?

buildup.text: Graceful degradation provides reduced functionality instead of total failure when a component is unavailable.

discovery.text: Amazon shows generic bestsellers when its recommendation engine fails. Users get a worse experience, not no experience.

twist.text: Degradation must be designed in advance. You can't decide what to show during an outage — it must be planned and tested.

climax.text: The best systems degrade so gracefully that most users never notice something is broken behind the scenes.

punchline.text: When something breaks, do less — not nothing.

quiz.question: What is graceful degradation?
options: Providing reduced functionality instead of total failure when a component breaks

hook.text: Your HTTP client has no timeout. The server hangs. Your request waits forever, holding a thread, connection, and memory.

buildup.text: Timeouts set a maximum wait time. If the server doesn't respond in 5 seconds, the client gives up and moves on.

discovery.text: Set two timeouts: a connection timeout (how long to establish contact) and a read timeout (how long to wait for data).

twist.text: Timeouts that are too short cause false failures on slow but successful requests. Too long and threads pile up waiting.

climax.text: Every network call needs a timeout. A missing timeout is a bug — it's an implicit decision to wait forever.

punchline.text: Always set timeouts — waiting forever is never acceptable.

quiz.question: Why are missing timeouts considered a bug?
options: They allow requests to wait forever, consuming resources indefinitely

hook.text: Your primary database crashes. A replica that's been silently syncing every second takes over in 30 seconds.

buildup.text: Active-passive: the primary handles all traffic. The passive replica stays in sync, ready to take over on failure.

discovery.text: Failover can be automatic (health check triggers it) or manual (a human decides). Automatic is faster but riskier.

twist.text: The replica might be slightly behind. Promoting it means losing the last few seconds of writes. Data loss is possible.

climax.text: Active-passive is the simplest redundancy pattern. It's the foundation of high availability for databases.

punchline.text: Primary handles traffic; passive is ready to take over on failure.

quiz.question: What is the risk of automatic failover?
options: The replica may be slightly behind, causing a few seconds of data loss
It's too slow to be useful
The passive replica can't handle traffic

hook.text: Both data centers handle traffic simultaneously. If one goes down, the other continues without any failover delay.

buildup.text: Active-active: multiple replicas all serve read and write traffic. No single primary — all nodes are equal.

discovery.text: Active-active eliminates failover delay. Users are already served by multiple locations — one disappearing is seamless.

twist.text: Write conflicts: two users update the same record in different data centers simultaneously. Which write wins?

climax.text: Active-active is powerful for availability but requires conflict resolution strategies for concurrent writes.

punchline.text: Both replicas serve traffic — no failover delay, but conflicts to manage.

quiz.question: What is the main challenge of active-active replication?
options: Resolving write conflicts when both replicas receive concurrent writes
Only one replica can serve reads

hook.text: An entire AWS region goes down. Your application keeps running because it's deployed in two regions.

buildup.text: Multi-region deploys your app in geographically separate data centers. If one region fails, others serve traffic.

discovery.text: DNS-based routing directs users to the nearest healthy region. Latency is lower and availability is higher.

twist.text: Keeping data consistent across regions is the hard part. Cross-region replication has latency — typically 50-200ms.

climax.text: Multi-region is the gold standard for high availability but adds significant complexity and cost.

punchline.text: Deploy in multiple regions — survive any single region failing.

quiz.question: What is the biggest challenge of multi-region architecture?
options: Keeping data consistent across regions with replication latency

hook.text: Your database is corrupted. Your last backup was 6 months ago. Six months of customer data — gone.

buildup.text: Full backups copy everything. Incremental backups copy only what changed since the last backup. Both are needed.

discovery.text: Point-in-time recovery uses transaction logs to restore the database to any specific second. Not just the last backup.

twist.text: Backups are worthless if never tested. Many teams discover their backups are corrupt only during an actual crisis.

climax.text: The 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, on 2 different media, with 1 offsite. Test restores regularly.

punchline.text: A backup that's never been tested is not a backup.

quiz.question: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
options: 3 copies, on 2 different media, with 1 stored offsite
Back up 3 times a day for 2 weeks

hook.text: A server crashes but the load balancer keeps sending it traffic. Users see errors for 5 minutes until someone notices.

buildup.text: Health checks are periodic probes: the load balancer asks each server 'are you alive?' every few seconds.

discovery.text: Shallow checks test if the process is running. Deep checks test if the database, cache, and dependencies are reachable.

twist.text: If checks are too deep, a dependency outage makes all servers report unhealthy — the load balancer removes them all.

climax.text: Health checks should be deep enough to catch real problems but not so deep that they cause false negatives.

punchline.text: Check if services are truly healthy — not just running.

quiz.question: What is the risk of overly deep health checks?
options: A dependency outage makes all servers appear unhealthy, removing them all

hook.text: It's 3 AM. Your phone buzzes: 'Error rate above 5%.' You have 15 minutes to acknowledge before it escalates.

buildup.text: On-call engineers carry a pager (now a phone app) and respond to production alerts within minutes, day or night.

discovery.text: Good alerts have clear severity: P1 (wake people up), P2 (fix today), P3 (fix this week). Not all alerts are urgent.

twist.text: Alert fatigue is real. If 90% of alerts are noise, engineers start ignoring all alerts — including critical ones.

climax.text: Every alert should be actionable. If you can't do anything about it, it's a log entry, not an alert.

punchline.text: Alert on what's actionable — every page should mean something.

quiz.question: What causes alert fatigue?
options: Too many non-actionable alerts cause engineers to ignore all alerts

hook.text: Production is down. Everyone is panicking, talking over each other, and trying different fixes simultaneously. Chaos.

buildup.text: Incident response assigns roles: commander (coordinates), communicator (updates stakeholders), and responders (fix).

discovery.text: The incident commander doesn't fix the problem — they coordinate. Keeping order during chaos is a full-time job.

twist.text: Communication matters as much as fixing. Stakeholders need updates every 15-30 minutes, even if nothing has changed.

climax.text: Structured incident response turns panicked chaos into coordinated recovery. Practice it before you need it.

punchline.text: Assign roles, communicate, coordinate — don't improvise during outages.

quiz.question: What is the incident commander's role?
options: Coordinating the response effort, not fixing the problem directly
Writing code to fix the issue

hook.text: An engineer pushed a bad config and caused a 4-hour outage. Do you blame them? Or fix the system that allowed it?

buildup.text: Blameless postmortems focus on systemic causes, not individual mistakes. The goal is learning, not punishment.

discovery.text: Why did the system allow this? Why didn't tests catch it? Why no rollback? Fix the process, not the person.

twist.text: If people are punished for incidents, they hide information. Postmortems become incomplete and mistakes repeat.

climax.text: Blameless culture creates psychological safety. Engineers report near-misses, share mistakes, and everyone learns.

punchline.text: Blame the system, not the person — fix the process.

quiz.question: Why are blameless postmortems more effective?
options: People share information openly when they won't be punished, enabling systemic fixes

hook.text: It's 3 AM, you're half awake, and the database is down. Do you remember the exact recovery steps? Probably not.

buildup.text: A runbook is a step-by-step guide for handling specific incidents: database failover, service restart, cache flush.

discovery.text: Good runbooks include: symptoms, diagnosis steps, fix steps, rollback procedures, and who to escalate to.

twist.text: Runbooks rot. Systems change but runbooks don't. Outdated runbooks are worse than none — they give false confidence.

climax.text: Keep runbooks linked to alerts. When an alert fires, the runbook for that specific scenario should be one click away.

punchline.text: Written steps for 3 AM — when your brain can't improvise.

quiz.question: Why do runbooks need regular updates?
options: Systems change and outdated runbooks give false confidence
New team members can't read old runbooks

hook.text: Your service is down. Customers flood support with 'is it just me?' A status page answers that question for everyone.

buildup.text: A public status page shows real-time system health: which services are up, degraded, or experiencing outages.

discovery.text: Proactive communication during outages reduces support tickets by up to 80%. Users just want to know you're aware.

twist.text: The status page must be hosted independently. If your servers are down, the status page must still be accessible.

climax.text: Transparent communication during incidents builds trust. Hiding outages destroys it faster than the outage itself.

punchline.text: Tell customers before they ask — host the status page independently.

quiz.question: Why must a status page be hosted independently?
options: If your main infrastructure is down, the status page must still be accessible
It loads faster on a separate server

hook.text: Netflix deliberately kills production servers during business hours. And their system keeps running perfectly.

buildup.text: Chaos engineering injects failures into production to verify the system handles them before real failures strike.

discovery.text: Chaos Monkey randomly kills instances. If the system survives, it's resilient. If not, they fix it before a real outage.

twist.text: Running experiments in staging isn't enough. Production has different traffic patterns, data volumes, and edge cases.

climax.text: Chaos engineering shifts from hoping the system is resilient to proving it is — through controlled experiments.

punchline.text: Break things on purpose — find weaknesses before real failures do.

quiz.question: Why does Netflix run Chaos Monkey in production?
options: To verify resilience under real conditions before actual failures occur

hook.text: Your team simulates a major outage. The primary database goes down. Can you recover in under 30 minutes? Let's find out.

buildup.text: A game day is a scheduled exercise where teams practice responding to simulated failures in a controlled environment.

discovery.text: Game days test not just technical systems but also human processes: communication, escalation, and decision-making.

twist.text: Most teams discover their runbooks are outdated, backups don't work, or failover is slower than expected.

climax.text: Game days build muscle memory. When a real incident happens, the team has already practiced the response.

punchline.text: Practice disasters before they happen — discover gaps safely.

quiz.question: What do game days typically reveal?
options: Outdated runbooks, broken backups, and slower-than-expected failover
That systems are always perfectly resilient

hook.text: You add 500ms of latency to every database call. Suddenly, timeouts cascade through 4 services. The system crumbles.

buildup.text: Fault injection deliberately introduces failures: latency, errors, packet loss, CPU exhaustion, or disk full.

discovery.text: AWS Fault Injection Simulator and Gremlin can inject failures into specific services without modifying application code.

twist.text: Injecting faults without a hypothesis is just breaking things. You need a prediction: 'the system should survive this.'

climax.text: Fault injection turns theoretical resilience into tested resilience. What you've never tested, you can't trust.

punchline.text: Inject failures deliberately — test what you claim to handle.

quiz.question: Why does fault injection require a hypothesis?
options: Without a prediction, you're just breaking things — not learning from the results

hook.text: An entire AWS region goes offline. Your RTO is 4 hours. Can you actually recover in 4 hours? Have you ever tried?

buildup.text: RTO is how fast you must recover. RPO is how much data loss you can accept. Together they define your DR requirements.

discovery.text: A DR plan documents: what to recover, in what order, who is responsible, and where the backups are.

twist.text: Most DR plans have never been tested. In a real disaster, teams find recovery takes 3x longer than estimated.

climax.text: A disaster recovery plan that hasn't been tested is just a document. Regular DR drills turn it into a reliable process.

punchline.text: Plan for disaster, practice recovery — don't discover gaps during a crisis.

quiz.question: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
options: RTO is how fast you recover; RPO is how much data loss you accept
RTO is for databases; RPO is for servers

hook.text: Tools don't make systems reliable. Culture does. If nobody cares about reliability, no tool will save you.

buildup.text: A reliability culture means every engineer thinks about failure modes, writes runbooks, and monitors their services.

discovery.text: Google's SRE model embeds reliability engineers in product teams. Reliability isn't separate — it's everyone's job.

twist.text: Reliability culture needs management support. If shipping features always beats fixing reliability, culture erodes.

climax.text: The most reliable systems are built by teams where reliability is valued as much as feature velocity.

punchline.text: Reliability is a culture, not a tool — everyone owns it.

quiz.question: What does Google's SRE model do?
options: Embeds reliability engineers in product teams so reliability is everyone's concern
